content.title: About
content.content: The chicken drumstick is the lower part of the leg, consisting of meat, bone, and skin. It is commonly cooked whole, often with the skin left on, which becomes crispy and flavorful when properly prepared.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple in dishes that require juiciness and rich flavor, such as barbecues, roasts, and fried chicken.
The skin is rich in collagen, which turns into a crunchy crust during cooking.
The NS (no‑fat grill) method preserves maximum taste and nutrients while reducing added fat.
Drumsticks can be split into thigh and lower leg portions for easy portioning.
Different cuisines treat drumsticks uniquely: Asian recipes often marinate them in soy sauce, while Western styles coat them with spices and bake.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken drumsticks provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals help maintain immune health and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Skin supplies healthy fats
items.content: When eaten in moderation, the skin offers monounsaturated fats and cholesterol needed for hormonal balance.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Drumsticks fit well into low‑carb dietary patterns.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked chicken may contain Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: High sodium in marinades
items.content: Excessively salty marinades can increase sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Chicken protein allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

items.title: Caloric skin
items.content: The skin adds calories and fat; those monitoring weight should consume it in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken drumsticks can be baked, fried, grilled (NS), or braised. When cooking with skin, pat it dry, lightly brush with oil, season, and cook until golden and crisp. Serve with vegetables, sauces, or as part of dishes like chicken wings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh drumsticks in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen drumsticks store at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen pieces in the fridge, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Mango (Mangifera indica) is a tropical stone fruit native to South Asia, with sweet, juicy, golden-orange flesh and a large flat pit. It has green, yellow, orange, or red skin depending on the variety and ripeness. Mangoes are eaten fresh and used in smoothies, salads, chutneys, desserts, and savory dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mangoes have been cultivated in South Asia for thousands of years.
Mango is the national fruit of India and a widely loved fruit in tropical regions around the world.
Mangoes are related to cashews and pistachios.
Hundreds of mango varieties exist, with differing flavors and textures.
The skin and sap of mango contain urushiol, the compound also found in poison ivy.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Mango provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Provides vitamin A
items.content: Mango contains carotenoids that the body can convert into vitamin A.

items.title: Contains folate and vitamin B6
items.content: These nutrients support cell function and metabolism.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Mango contributes fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Mango contains plant compounds such as mangiferin with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Mango is naturally sweet, so portions matter for people monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Skin and sap reactions
items.content: People who are sensitive to poison ivy may develop a rash from contact with mango skin or sap.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people may be allergic to mango.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Eating a lot of mango, or unripe mango, may cause stomach upset in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mango can be peeled, sliced, or cubed and eaten fresh, blended into smoothies and lassi, added to salads and salsas, or cooked into chutneys and desserts. Unripe green mango is used in savory dishes and pickles. A ripe mango smells fruity near the stem and yields slightly to pressure.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unripe mangoes at room temperature until they soften and smell sweet. Ripe mangoes can be refrigerated for a few days. Cut mango should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator or frozen in chunks.

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed vegetables with added fat is a mixture of various vegetables (carrot, potato, onion, pepper, zucchini, etc.) slowly cooked in a modest amount of vegetable or animal fat. The dish has a rich aroma, tender texture, and a vivid flavor while retaining most of its vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stewing preserves more nutrients compared with prolonged boiling.
A small amount of fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
Stewed vegetables are a staple in many Eastern European and Mediterranean cuisines.
When cooked properly, vegetables keep their natural colour and aroma.
Stewed vegetables can serve as a base for soups, ragouts and casseroles.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Vegetables provide vitamin C, vitamin A (as beta‑carotene) and B‑vitamins that support immunity and vision.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains potassium, magnesium and iron, essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: A modest amount of healthy fat together with vegetables can help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals such as lycopene and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy to specific vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to certain vegetables (e.g., peppers or tomatoes).

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Excessive added fat raises the calorie count, which may be undesirable for weight management.

items.title: Vitamin C loss
items.content: Prolonged stewing can degrade some vitamin C, so avoid overcooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed vegetables can be served as a side dish, accompaniment to meat or fish, used as a filling for pies, added to salads or soups. Fresh herbs and spices can be added to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions – the dish retains flavor and nutrients for 2‑3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Zwieback toast is a dry, lightly toasted bread made from leavened dough. It has a crisp crust and a light, porous interior with a mildly sweet taste. The toast is often used as a base for sandwiches, snacks, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Zwieback originated in Germany in the 19th century as a way to extend the shelf life of bread.
It is commonly used in baby foods because it is easy to digest and rarely causes allergies.
Traditionally it is served with milk, compote, or jam.
In Russia the product is known as “sukhari” or “hard bread”.
Zwieback can be produced sweet or neutral, depending on added ingredients.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Zwieback provides quickly digestible carbs that supply energy.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Compared with many baked goods, zwieback contains little fat.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Its porous structure offers a modest amount of fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Zwieback provides thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, which aid metabolism.

items.title: Easy to prepare
items.content: The toast cooks quickly and can be incorporated into a variety of dishes.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Zwieback is made from wheat and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of fast‑absorbing carbs, it may cause a rapid rise in blood sugar.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: Some versions contain sugar, preservatives or flavorings that may not be suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Zwieback can be eaten dry, soaked in milk, used as a base for sandwiches, served with cottage cheese, jam, honey, or incorporated into recipes such as casseroles and desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the toast in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage keep it in the refrigerator to prevent mold growth.
